opus-5.5.text:
I see it as a flywheel, and the different pieces really need each other to grow.

Physical AI is the brain: models that understand the physical world, reason about it, and decide what actions to take. Robots are the body. A brain without a body can't do much in the real world, and a body without a good brain is just a very expensive machine doing narrow, pre-programmed tasks. For a long time robotics was stuck there. Every robot was engineered for one job in one environment, so the market stayed small and fragmented.

What's changing now is that we can build general-purpose models for the physical world. In my team's work on world foundation models, the goal is to give developers a model that has learned how the world works: how objects move, how things interact, what happens when you push something. With that, a robotics company doesn't have to start from scratch. They can take a pretrained model, post-train it on their own data and their own robot, and get to a useful product much faster. That lowers the barrier to entry, so more companies can build robots and more robots get deployed.

The mutual benefit comes from the loop that creates. More deployed robots generate more real-world data and reveal more failure cases. That data and feedback make the models better. Better models make robots more capable and more reliable, which opens new applications, which brings in more investment and more deployment. Each side pulls the other forward.

Data is the key bottleneck here. In language AI we had the internet. In physical AI we don't have an internet-scale dataset of robot interactions. So simulation and world models matter a lot: you can generate synthetic experience, test policies safely, and cover rare or dangerous scenarios you'd never want to collect in the real world. But simulation has to be grounded in reality, and the grounding comes from real robots out in the field. So again, the two depend on each other.

From the perspective of a company like NVIDIA, our role is to build the platform: the compute, the simulation tools, the foundation models. Then we make them open and accessible so the ecosystem can build on top. We don't build every robot ourselves. If the whole ecosystem succeeds, the market gets bigger for everyone, including us. I think that's the healthiest way for a new industry to develop. Nobody can solve physical AI alone. It's too big and too hard. It needs researchers, model builders, hardware makers, and application companies all pushing at the same time.

So my view is that this isn't a zero-sum game. We're still at a very early stage, maybe similar to where language models were several years ago. The most important thing right now is to grow the pie, to get the technology working well enough that robots become genuinely useful in factories, warehouses, homes, and hospitals. Once that happens, I think the value created will be enormous, and there will be plenty of room for many players to benefit.

r001.rationale: The response describes researchers, model builders, hardware makers, and application companies working together, with deployed robots and better models reinforcing each other to grow the market.

r002.rationale: It says NVIDIA provides compute and benefits if the ecosystem succeeds, but does not identify robot sales as a source of demand that generates revenue for compute providers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it as a flywheel, honestly. When I look at physical AI and robotics, the thing that becomes obvious very quickly is that no single company can do all of it. You need the chips, you need the simulation, you need the foundation models, you need the robot hardware, you need the people who actually deploy these systems in factories and warehouses and hospitals. That's an enormous stack, and nobody owns the whole thing.

So the way we think about it is: what layer can we contribute where we really have an advantage, and how do we make everyone else in the ecosystem more successful? For us, that's the compute and the simulation platform and the world foundation models, things like Cosmos. We spend a lot of effort building those because the physical world is incredibly hard to collect data from. You can't just scrape the internet for robot experience the way you did for language. So if we can generate realistic, physically grounded synthetic data and give it to the robot companies, suddenly their models get better faster, they ship sooner, and the market grows.

And when the market grows, it comes back to us. More robots in the world means more demand for training compute, more demand for inference at the edge, more demand for simulation. It's genuinely mutual. Their success is our success. I'm not saying that as a slogan, it's just how the economics work out.

The other thing I'd say is that the market is so early that competition is almost the wrong frame. Right now the enemy is not another robotics company, the enemy is the difficulty of the problem itself. Robots that generalize, that can operate safely among people, that don't need a PhD to reprogram. If a dozen companies all get meaningfully better at that, the pie expands for all of us. There will be a time to fight over slices, but that's not where we are. Right now, if we can help a startup train a humanoid policy in weeks instead of years, that's good for them, good for us, and frankly good for the world.

r001.rationale: The response says companies contribute across the ecosystem so robotics firms can improve and ship sooner, which grows the market for everyone.

r002.rationale: It says more robots in the world create more demand for training compute, edge inference, and simulation, and that this demand comes back to the compute and simulation provider.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a reinforcing cycle. Physical AI gives robots the ability to perceive, reason, and act in more complex environments. As those capabilities improve, robots become useful for more tasks, which creates a larger market. And as more robots are deployed, we learn more about the problems that actually matter: where the models fail, what reliability is required, and what makes a system economically useful. That feedback helps us build better AI.

But the mutual benefit also comes from the ecosystem. The AI developers need robotics companies that understand hardware and control. Robotics companies need partners who understand the customer’s workflow. And customers need a solution that delivers enough value to justify adopting it. So I would think about this as building those capabilities together, starting with applications where we can demonstrate clear value and then expanding from there.

r001.rationale: It describes AI developers, robotics companies, and customers building capabilities together, starting with valuable applications and expanding the market.

r002.rationale: It says robot deployments provide feedback that improves AI, but does not identify robot sales as demand that generates revenue for compute providers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think physical AI and robotics can help each other grow. Better AI makes robots more capable and useful, and putting robots into real environments gives us feedback about where the AI still needs to improve.

The key is to start with tasks where the robot can deliver clear value. If it helps a customer do something more safely or reliably, that creates demand. More deployment then supports further investment in the models, hardware, and tools.

So building the technology and building the market have to happen together. You learn what matters by working with customers, and those lessons help you build better technology.

r001.rationale: It says building the technology and market must happen together, with customer deployment and feedback helping both grow.

r002.rationale: It says deployments create demand and support investment, but does not identify compute providers as recipients of revenue.
